newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico economic goals possible - Morgan economist.
newsitem.headline: Mexico economic goals possible - Morgan economist.

text.p: Mexico's economic goals of annual five percent economic growth and an increase in overall investment to 25 percent of GDP by the year 2000 are both possible to reach, Morgan Stanley Dean Witter economist Ernest "Chip" Brown said in a report on Wednesday.
On Tuesday, Mexico's President Ernesto Zedillo outlined a new economic plan stretching to the turn of the century.

The National Program for Financing Development aims at five percent growth on average each year, as well as targetting annual inflation of 7.5 percent and a current account deficit of 3.2 percent of GDP (gross domestic product) by the year 2000.

"It is political heresy in Mexico to aspire to growth of less than 5 percent, but if the Zedillo government plays the right cards, 5 percent growth is certainly possible," wrote Brown, Morgan's senior economist for Latin America.

"A second goal, given nearly equal prominence, is to raise the overall investment rate from 22 percent of GDP this year to 25 percent in 2000. This is to be financed by raising the savings rate in the economy. We think that this is also possible if the right steps are taken," the New York-based Brown wrote in a report made available in Mexico City.

One such step would be to encourage domestic banks to sharply raise loan-loss provisions and capitalization levels as well as "get on with the business of being financial intermediaries, not merely repositories for old stocks of troubled loans."
He noted that the assumed rate of consumption spending will rise faster than expected import growth to the year 2000 in the program.
"About the only way that this is going to happen, we think, is if the rate of devaluation of the Mexican peso picks up," Brown said.
